claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
The GeoDeploy example project is hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API documentation is located at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
The TypeSafe Jev documentation is located at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
GeoDeploy picks the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for a user's workload.
GeoDeploy gates every AI decision on confidence.
GeoDeploy provisions Kubernetes for the user.
GeoDeploy is open source and available today.
GeoDeploy prices every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list so that Jev cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy gates every decision on confidence, with hard rejects for data residency.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters with one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy can scale itself in a self-driving mode, with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the past week (relative to this post's 2026-09-25 publish date).
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
GeoDeploy is a Pulumi example hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy's design, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math, but never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy's design, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy's design, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, but never decides anything.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's TypeScript logic deterministically bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.
Jev picks the winning region and modules for each geo in GeoDeploy's pipeline.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules including EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API is documented at /automation/.
GeoDeploy's provisioning step runs a Pulumi preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy's provisioning step will not run at all unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md file containing the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev does not return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence score.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels for its rubrics.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets, choosing among region IDs that GeoDeploy has already priced and checked.
Jev never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture.

In a single call, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection via choice(), five quality scores via score() (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency), two hard checks via noul() (data residency and capacity), and a fallback region via choice().

The file packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repository contains a buildStageAQuestions function that imports choice, noul, and score from @typesafe-ai/sdk and constructs selection, coverage, costFit, residencyOk, and fallback questions as shown.
The options passed to Jev's choice() function are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."

GeoDeploy's coverage rubric has 10 levels, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

The GeoDeploy code sends the whole question set to Jev in one call via client.systemOne(), along with the state Jev reasons over, and returns answers such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
The five quality scores feed a ranking system in GeoDeploy that runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's WEIGHT_PROFILES constant defines exact weight values for cost, coverage, maturity, sprawl, and archConsistency across the latency-optimized, balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain profiles as shown in the code block.
In GeoDeploy's ranking formula, sprawl risk is subtracted from the composite score because every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider, such that AWS always means EKS and ECR.
GeoDeploy leaves Jev to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier as open module choices.
In GeoDeploy, every Jev answer is checked against a confidence threshold matched to how risky the decision is.
In GeoDeploy, the data residency decision has a confidence threshold of 0.95, below which it hard-rejects.
In GeoDeploy, the region-for-a-new-cluster decision has a confidence threshold of 0.90, below which the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
In GeoDeploy, the region-when-a-stack-already-exists decision has a confidence threshold of 0.75, below which the existing region is kept.
In GeoDeploy, the ingress-or-autoscaling-module decision has a confidence threshold of 0.85, below which the registry default is used.
In GeoDeploy, the node-pool-sizing-tier decision has a confidence threshold of 0.60, below which the bin-packing result is used.
In GeoDeploy, the global confidence floor for region pick, residency, or capacity decisions is 0.50, below which the AI path is dropped for that geo.

The file packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the GeoDeploy repository contains a residency gate check and a candidate-selection validation check as shown in the code block, where residencyOk is enforced as a hard gate against GATE_THRESHOLDS.residencyOk and throws an AiPathAborted error if the selection is not among the shortlisted candidates.
Each AiPathAborted error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled via the `geodeploy monitor` command.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy's agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with possible answers no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is applied automatically above 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is suggested for a human to approve when confidence is between 0.70 and 0.85.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric, and once a traffic baseline is established, it is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or an application-specific signal.
Pulumi's X account handle is @PulumiCorp, reachable at https://x.com/PulumiCorp.
Users can sign up for a free Pulumi account at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
Access to Jev and a cloud provider are the only prerequisites to getting started with GeoDeploy today.
